summary.text: The Poisson distribution gives the probability of a given number of events in a fixed interval when they occur at a known constant mean rate, independently of the time since the last event.
Its parameter λ equals both the expected value and the variance, and it can describe counts in an area or volume as well as in time.
It suits many possible events that are each rare, but fails when the rate changes or events are not independent, such as students arriving in groups.

facts.label: Classic example
facts.value: Radioactive decay events during a fixed observation period

facts.label: Horse kicks
facts.value: In 1898 Bortkiewicz modelled Prussian soldiers killed by horse kicks

facts.label: Earlier result
facts.value: Abraham de Moivre gave similar results in 1711

items.prompt: A count follows a Poisson distribution with an average of 4. What is its variance?
items.explain: The parameter λ is equal to both the expected value and the variance: λ = E (X) = Var (X).

items.prompt: A student union counts arrivals each minute. The rate is low during class and high between classes, and friends tend to walk in together. Why is a plain Poisson model a poor fit?

options.label: The count is too large for any distribution
The rate is not constant and arrivals are not independent
Poisson models only apply to radioactive decay
Students never arrive in a fixed interval of time

items.explain: The rate is not constant and arrivals of individual students are not independent, since students tend to come in groups.

items.prompt: The number of magnitude 5 earthquakes in a country per year may not be Poisson distributed. What could break the assumptions?

options.label: Earthquakes can only be counted once a decade
Earthquakes are far too rare to count at all
A large quake can raise the chance of aftershocks
A year is too short to be an interval

items.explain: If one large earthquake increases the probability of aftershocks, events are not independent of each other.

items.prompt: A forest is divided into equal square plots, and an ecologist counts trees in each plot. Can a Poisson distribution be considered?

options.label: Yes, since it can describe counts in an area, not only time
No, because Poisson counts only work over time intervals
No, because trees are too numerous to count
Yes, but only if every plot has exactly one tree

items.explain: The distribution can be used for events in other kinds of intervals, such as a given area, and tree locations are an example.

items.prompt: A system has a huge number of possible events, each of them rare, and you count how many happen in a fixed time. Which distribution can fit under the right circumstances?

options.label: A distribution where all counts are equally likely
A distribution with a single certain count
A distribution that always peaks at zero
A Poisson distribution

items.explain: The Poisson distribution can be applied to systems with a large number of possible events, each of which is rare.

items.prompt: You only ever record visits where at least one event is guaranteed to happen. Is a plain Poisson distribution right?

options.label: Yes, since a guaranteed event is a rare event
No, such counts may be modelled by a zero-truncated Poisson
Yes, as long as the rate is at least one
No, since such counts can never be modelled

items.explain: Examples where at least one event is guaranteed are not Poisson distributed, but can be modelled with a zero-truncated Poisson.
